turns.prompt_text: if I run the API, A.I. Of Gemini and I ask it a bunch of questions. Does it keep context, or do I need to do that some other way?
turns.response_html:
When using the Gemini API, the model itself is technically stateless. This means that if you simply send a single prompt, the API does not "remember" what you said in previous requests. To maintain a conversation, you have to manage the context yourself.

Here is how it works and the methods available to handle context:

1. Manual History Management

The most common way to maintain context is to pass the entire conversation history back to the API with every new prompt. You send a list of messages (alternating between "user" and "model" roles), and the model processes that entire list to generate the next response.

  • Pros: Complete control over what the model remembers.
  • Cons: As the conversation grows, you use more tokens, which increases costs and can eventually hit the model's context window limit.

2. The ChatSession Object (SDKs)

If you are using the official Google AI Python, Node.js, or Go SDKs, there is a built-in start_chat method. This creates a ChatSession object that handles the history for you locally.

  • It automatically appends your new questions and the model’s answers to an internal list.
  • Note: This is still just a "helper" on your side of the code; it is still sending the full history to the API behind the scenes.

3. Context Caching (For Large Data)

For very long conversations or massive datasets (like a 500-page PDF or an hour-long video), Gemini offers Context Caching.

  • Instead of sending a massive amount of data with every single turn, you "cache" the initial context on Google's servers for a set period.
  • This significantly reduces costs and latency for repetitive high-token queries.

4. System Instructions

To keep the model's "personality" or "rules" consistent without repeating them in every user message, you use the system_instruction parameter. This is a separate block of text that tells the AI how to behave (e.g., "Act like a helpful lab assistant") and remains the foundation for every turn in that session.

Comparison Table

FeatureDoes it keep context?Best for...
Standard API CallNoOne-off tasks or "stateless" requests.
ChatSession (SDK)YesStandard multi-turn chatbots.
Context CachingYesQueries involving massive documents or long histories.
System InstructionYesDefining permanent behavior/rules for the session.

In short: If you are building an app, you are responsible for storing the conversation (usually in a database or a local array) and feeding it back to Gemini so it knows what you're talking about.

Handling a "project history" without sending the full conversation back and forth every time is actually one of the most significant shifts in the Gemini ecosystem for 2026. You are essentially looking for persistent context rather than session-based history.

Here is how you can manage large project-specific intelligence without drowning the API in history logs:

1. Agent Memory Bank & Memory Profiles

Google recently introduced the Agent Memory Bank. Unlike a standard chat session that resets when the window closes, this creates a long-term storage layer.

  • Memory Profiles: You can create a "Memory Profile" specifically for your project. This acts as a persistent repository of high-accuracy details (project goals, tech stack, past decisions) that the agent can recall across different sessions over months.
  • How it works: Instead of sending the history, the agent dynamically fetches relevant "memories" from this bank with low latency.

2. "Projects" in Gemini Enterprise

If you are working in a team or enterprise environment, the Projects feature centralizes context.

  • It creates a shared workspace where the agent maintains a permanent "brain" for that specific endeavor.
  • It creates a shared source of truth (often via specialized files like project_overview.md or architecture.md) that the agent treats as its foundational reality every time you re-engage.

3. Context Caching (The Cost-Saver)

For massive technical docs or codebases (up to 1M+ tokens), you can use Context Caching.

  • You "freeze" your project's technical manuals or core codebase into the model's active memory.
  • This data stays on Google's servers. When you ask a question, the API only processes your new question against the cached project context.
  • The Benefit: It’s roughly 90% cheaper than sending that massive data block with every prompt.

4. RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)

For truly enormous projects (e.g., thousands of files), you would use a Vector Database (like Vertex AI Search or BigQuery).

  • Instead of the model "remembering" everything, you store the project data in a searchable database.
  • When you ask a question, a system first searches your project files for relevant snippets and feeds only those few snippets to Gemini. This is the most scalable way to handle "infinite" history.

Which should you use?

A massive codebase/manualContext Caching
A huge database of documentationRAG / Vector Search
A collaborative team effortGemini Enterprise Projects

The Tiered Architecture

The system is organized into three distinct cognitive layers, each with a specific scope of authority and data access:

  1. The Manager (Policy & Budget Layer):

    • Responsibility: Strategic oversight and financial guardrails.
    • Context: Maintains the "Project Ledger," tracking total token expenditure and time-to-completion metrics.
    • Logic: Uses a high-level decision matrix to determine if a "chapter" is successful or if a pivot is required. It does not see granular logs; it only sees the Assistant's summarized reports.
    • Formula: The Manager monitors the budget $B$ where $B_{remaining} = B_{total} - \sum_{i=1}^{n} (T_{i} \times C)$, where $T$ is tokens used per turn and $C$ is the cost per token.

  2. The Assistant (Operations & Lifecycle Layer):

    • Responsibility: Process orchestration and specialist management.
    • Context: Maintains the "Active Workspace State." It tracks the status of specialist worker bees, manages their initialization, and shuts them down to conserve local RAM and token costs.
    • Reporting: Periodically synthesizes specialist activity into a structured report for the Manager, highlighting blockers or unexpected resource spikes.

  3. The Specialist (Execution & Tooling Layer):

    • Responsibility: Task execution via local system interaction.
    • Tooling: Utilizes the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to gain secure, standardized access to the Mac Mini's file system, terminal, and local applications.
    • Lifecycle: These agents are ephemeral. They exist only for the duration of a specific task (e.g., "Refactor the login module") and are purged once the Assistant validates the work.

Implementation on the Mac Mini

For a Mac Mini environment, LangGraph or a custom Python State Machine is recommended over traditional linear chains. This allows for the "alternate and check-in" logic the user described.

The Assistant follows a Cyclical Execution Pattern:

  1. Initialize: Assistant spawns a Specialist with a specific sub-task.
  2. Execution Loop: The Specialist performs 2–3 turns of work (calling local tools via MCP).
  3. Intervention: The Assistant pauses the Specialist, retrieves the stdout or file changes, and performs a "Sanity Check."
  4. Reporting: After a set number of check-ins, the Assistant aggregates the findings and presents the "Chapter Update" to the Manager.

The Token-Time Continuum

In a multi-project matrix, the Work-Period acts as the temporal container (e.g., a 24-hour cycle), while the Movement defines the specific quantum of effort. The user’s observation that the exhaustion rate remains constant regardless of the number of active projects implies a Synchronous Throttle logic.

The math governing this "constant burn" can be expressed as: $$R_{global} = \sum_{p=1}^{n} \dot{T}_p = K$$ Where:

  • $R_{global}$ is the global token exhaustion rate (tokens/minute).
  • $\dot{T}_p$ is the rate of consumption for Project $p$.
  • $K$ is the hard throttle constant defined by the API rate limits or the user’s budget.

If only one project has a "Movement" scheduled, $\dot{T}_p = K$. If eight projects are running, $\dot{T}_p = \frac{K}{8}$. This ensures the system never spikes into a rate-limit violation and maintains a predictable "heartbeat" across the entire infrastructure.

The Hierarchical Priority Queue

To manage 8+ projects over a week or a month, the Assistant Agent must operate as a Priority Multiplexer. It views the project landscape as a sheet of music where each "measure" is a token slice.

Agent LevelRole in the QueueAction
ManagerComposerAssigns the number of movements and token ceilings ($L_M$) to each project per work-period.
AssistantConductorManages the "Breathing" between projects, ensuring the sum of active movements respects the constant $K$.
SpecialistPerformerExecutes the 2–3 turn "Verses" until the assigned movement's tokens are spent or the task is finished.

When a project has 0 movements assigned for a work-period, it is effectively "Resting." This allows the Assistant to reallocate that project's slice of $K$ to more urgent "Movements" in other projects, accelerating their completion without increasing the daily budget risk.

The "Purge and Pivot" Logic

In this framework, the Recent History serves as the "Short-Term Memory" of the movement.

  • During the Movement: The Assistant maintains a sliding window of $D$ turns. This allows the Specialist to maintain continuity on a specific task (e.g., debugging a function).
  • Post-Movement: Once the movement objectives are met or the token limit is reached, the Assistant generates a Consolidated State Update.
  • The Pivot: The Manager reviews this update, navigates the project toward its next goal, and triggers the history_purge. The next movement begins with a "Clean Breath," carrying only the high-level state from the Manager’s navigation.

Dynamic History Depth ($D$)

The Assistant and Manager agents can dynamically adjust the depth $D \in {1, 2}$ based on the complexity of the current task. This optimization balances context richness against the daily token budget.

The token overhead for history ($T_{h}$) for any given request is calculated as: $$T_{h} \approx \sum_{i=1}^{D} (L_{u,i} + L_{m,i})$$ Where:

  • $L_{u,i}$ is the length of the user prompt at turn $i$.
  • $L_{m,i}$ is the length of the model response at turn $i$.

If the Specialist is performing routine file operations, $D=1$ suffices. If the task involves complex logic refactoring, the Assistant may elevate $D=2$ to ensure the agent doesn't "lose the thread" of the previous change.
